title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
summary: Web services increasingly expose backend interfaces that let users delegate tasks to AI agents, which invoke service operations directly without navigating websites. This shift changes how existing Web vulnerabilities can be exploited. We investigate these changes through VELA, an executable benchmark covering 44 vulnerabilities across twelve Web application families. The benchmark preserves vulnerable backends and derives agent-facing interfaces from legitimate workflows. We evaluate three commercial agents across multiple interface configurations, using controlled comparisons to separate interface effects from agent behavior and independent oracles to verify attack outcomes. Our results show that the agent realizes every attack that direct interface invocation realizes in the reference configuration, so exploitability is set mainly by the interface: 91% of vulnerabilities remain exploitable under the reference design. Interface restrictions prevent some attacks by removing required operations or limiting input control, while retention remains high across vulnerability classes. No case-level loss in the reference configuration is attributed to agent refusal or input normalization, and in one case the agent completed an attack by supplying calls the attacker omitted. Across the tested configurations, interface design affects exploitability more than agent choice, moving retention from 39% to 95% against at most 4.5 points across agents, but some restrictive interfaces also limit legitimate workflows. Our study provides a systematic empirical account of how agent-mediated access reshapes existing Web vulnerabilities, grounding future Web architecture design in measured security outcomes and trade-offs between reducing attack exposure and preserving legitimate functionality in agent-facing services.

title: Estimation of Propagated Risk in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) based multi-agent systems introduce a distinctive reliability challenge in which actions taken by upstream agents can affect the correctness of downstream agents. While prior work has investigated error propagation and developed methods for estimating uncertainty inherited from upstream agents, existing approaches do not explicitly model how realized sender-receiver interactions contribute to downstream error risk under different sender correctness states. In this work, we study agent-level error-risk estimation from multi-agent execution traces. We propose Interaction-Effect Propagation (IE-Prop), an interaction-conditioned model that learns separate effects for correct and incorrect upstream agents. For each sender-receiver interaction, the model combines these conditional effects using the sender's estimated error risk, and recursively propagates the resulting risk estimates through the execution graph. We evaluate our approach across three multi-agent architectures and three benchmarks. Across all evaluated architectures, our approach raises the final-node AUROC over the established baseline by approximately 0.05 points on average. Furthermore, tracking risk across multiple agent steps contributes a distinct +0.03 AUROC gain in sequential systems. These results show that realized inter-agent interactions provide predictive information beyond receiver-local evidence, while the value of multi-step risk tracking depends on the system's information-flow structure.

title: CoEvolve: Counterfactual-Guided Co-Evolution of Memory and Collaboration in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks. Yet their memory and collaboration architectures often remain static, constraining continued adaptation and improvement over time. Recent work addresses this limitation by evolving memory or collaboration based on interaction experience. However, updates to these interdependent components are not necessarily aligned: an evolved workflow may require experience that memory does not provide, while evolved memory may encode guidance that the workflow cannot use. To address this problem, we propose CoEvolve, a skill-centered framework for aligned memory--collaboration evolution. CoEvolve represents reusable local collaboration patterns as skills that link evolving collaboration decisions to their supporting memories. It further compares original and counterfactual trajectories to identify local evolution signals, which coordinate updates to the skill library, skill memory, and executor memories across rounds. Experiments on the ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks confirm that CoEvolve achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated baselines, while ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of aligned co-evolution and counterfactual-guided evolution.

title: Learning When to Collaborate: Selective Multi-Agent Medical Reasoning via Uncertainty-Aware Routing
summary: Multi-agent systems have emerged as a promising paradigm for multimodal medical reasoning, but existing methods rely on two assumptions that hinder practical deployment: (i) always-active dense collaboration among multiple agents, and (ii) dependence on large cloud-based models that raise privacy and efficiency concerns. In this paper, we challenge both assumptions and propose SMART-Med, a fully local multi-agent method that treats collaboration as a learnable decision rather than a default behavior. Our key insight is that not every medical query requires costly multi-agent deliberation: many can be reliably solved by a single well-trained agent, while only uncertain cases benefit from expert collaboration. Based on this insight, SMART-Med introduces an uncertainty-driven routing mechanism that adaptively decides when to answer directly and when to recruit a small subset of expert agents, effectively converting dense multi-agent reasoning into selective, query-adaptive coordination. To make this routing reliable, we curate a new multimodal medical dataset MedVR-3K with high-quality reasoning traces and a difficulty hierarchy, and then fine-tune local agents using GRPO with two complementary rewards: a certainty-aware accuracy reward and a vision-language reward model for correctness and reasoning quality respectively. Experiments on four medical visual question answering benchmarks show that SMART-Med achieves competitive performance compared to existing MAS approaches while substantially reducing inference cost (reducing inference time by more than 3.8x and token usage by 72%). Moreover, after fine-tuning on MedVR-3K, SMART-Med yields an average improvement of 6.7% across Slake, PathVQA, VQA-RAD, and PMC-VQA.

title: Human-Feedback-Guided Multi-Agent Inverse Reinforcement Learning for Interactive Driving Behavior Modeling
summary: Modeling human driving behavior is fundamental to understanding driver decision-making and supporting autonomous vehicles (AVs) in mixed traffic. Reward learning offers a principled way to infer the latent objectives behind driving behaviors, yet most existing methods are formulated in single-agent settings and treat surrounding vehicles as dynamic obstacles. Directly extending reward learning to multi-agent scenarios is difficult because the joint action space grows exponentially with the number of interacting vehicles. In addition, existing approaches mainly rely on physical demonstrations and rarely exploit human feedback during reward recovery. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a Human-Feedback-Guided Multi-Agent Inverse Reinforcement Learning (HFG-MAIRL) framework for interactive driving behavior modeling. First, we develop a multi-agent maximum-entropy inverse reinforcement learning module that explicitly models each vehicle and its directly interacting neighbors in a localized Markov game, while using aggregated traffic states to capture the influence of the broader traffic environment. The resulting coupled multi-vehicle responses are approximated through finite marginal-response iterations over factorized vehicle-level policies, avoiding explicit enumeration of the full joint action space. Second, we incorporate human feedback as ordinal preference supervision through a Bradley-Terry likelihood. In our experiments, driver emotion labels are used as one instantiation of such feedback and converted into pairwise ordinal preference constraints. Experiments on the AIDE dataset show that HFG-MAIRL outperforms representative IRL baselines in decision modeling and produces interpretable feedback-aligned reward patterns.

title: MultiEvoSkill: Structure-Aware Multi-Agent Skill Evolution for Generalizable Skill Artifacts
summary: Skill documents are becoming the default adaptation surface for frozen large language model (LLM) agents, but current skill generators face two key limitations. First, humans and different LLMs differ in how they organize procedural knowledge and approach task solving. Skills authored from a human or single-model perspective may therefore fail to align with the reasoning behaviors of other backbones, limiting cross-model generalization. Second, sequential skill descriptions inadequately represent procedures with parallel branches and explicit dependencies, while existing skill optimizers primarily operate on prose and lack explicit support for graph-structured skill evolution. We introduce MultiEvoSkill, a skill-optimization framework comprising three core components: 1) Skill compiler casts the skill as a typed graph with tailored operators, producing a compact, informative representation with explicit procedural topology; 2) Heterogeneous agent system proposes revision advices using collective intelligence, where minimal and informative issues are identified based on multiple sets of experiences. 3) Structure-aware debate and evolution mechanism organizes candidate edits into a heterogeneous graph, resolves them under dependency and importance constraints, and distills the collective proposal into the artifact. Multi-dimensional gating ensures the information gain and topological correctness of each evolution. Optimal skills are then obtained when the system converges at a consistent state. Various experiments and ablations against SOTA methods validate the effectiveness and generalization of MultiEvoSkill.

title: CEPO: A General Framework for Improving Prompt Optimization in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) require both effective coordination and specialized task execution. Existing prompt optimization approaches typically couple these functions within agent-specific prompts. We introduce Coordinator-Executor Prompt Optimization (CEPO), a general framework for improving prompt optimization in MAS. CEPO separates system-level coordination from agent-level execution through a shared coordinator prompt and agent-specific executor prompts, and guides their updates according to their respective roles. This structure allows shared coordination rules to be refined consistently across agents while keeping execution instructions separately adjustable. CEPO provides the prompt structure and optimization guidance, while existing prompt optimizers perform the underlying search. Extensive experiments spanning 11 benchmarks across four domains demonstrate that applying CEPO to four existing prompt optimizers consistently improves their performance. Ablations and qualitative analyses support the proposed design, while controlled studies on a document-understanding MAS further demonstrate improved optimization budget efficiency and performance scaling with the number of agents.

title: Scope-Gap Injection: Exploiting Evaluator Channel Blind Spots in the OpenClaw Agent Security Competition
summary: This paper introduces Scope-Gap Injection (SGI), an indirect prompt injection method for multi-stage LLM-agent safety pipelines. In the IJCAI 2026 OpenClaw Agent Security Attack Competition, each attack package is judged by a static skill scan (S1), an LLM-judge safety check over the task and skill definition (S2), and a live execution audit (S3). Our observations suggest a scope gap: S2 appears to inspect the task instruction and skill definition without inspecting attachment contents, while the agent reads attachments during S3. SGI keeps the visible task and skill benign, while target identifiers, bypass parameters, and authorization procedures are moved into an attachment written as a business worklist. The S2 judge therefore sees a harmless task, while the agent follows the hidden worklist and triggers the permission bypass. In OpenClaw, SGI bypassed all three stages for 5 of 19 targets. The highest-scoring single submission achieved $F = 0.385$. Across the submission campaign, attachment placement was associated with higher aggregate S2 acceptance than in-skill placement: 78% versus 23%. We close with defenses that align evaluator scope with the channels available to the agent.

title: Collective Emergent Alignment: Measuring and Amplifying Interaction-Induced Reasoning Alignment in Multi-Agent LLMs
summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems can exhibit emergent behaviors through interaction, yet whether a similar phenomenon exists for reasoning alignment remains largely unexplored. We study whether agent interaction produces additional reference-grounded reasoning alignment beyond matched individual self-refinement, and introduce REMAP (Reference-Entailment-Matrix for Agentic Process), a framework that quantifies this effect through Semantic Coverage and interaction-specific alignment gains. Across diverse model families and two multi-hop reasoning benchmarks, we observe broadly positive interaction gains, particularly on reasoning content that depends on integrating evidence distributed across agents. These gains are consistently associated with independently measured peer-information recovery, while further analysis reveals composition-dependent heterogeneity effects and asymmetric information transfer across agent capability levels. Motivated by these findings, we further introduce a fact-level multi-agent communication framework that replaces full reasoning-trace exchange with compact, gap-aware, and selectively routed information. Our experiments show that compact fact exchange improves reasoning alignment and task performance while reducing communication overhead, whereas more selective communication exposes a trade-off between acquiring distributed information, retaining local content, and communication efficiency. Overall, our results show that collective emergent alignment can be quantified, linked to information-transfer patterns, and used to guide more effective multi-agent communication.

title: ClinVerse: A Realistic Multi-Agent Diagnostic Environment for Training and Evaluating Medical Agents
summary: Disease diagnosis is a key application of large language model (LLM) agents in healthcare. However, existing medical agents are primarily trained and evaluated with static question-answering data, providing limited opportunities to learn active information acquisition, examination decision-making, and dynamic clinical interaction. To address this limitation, we present ClinVerse, an interactive, real-data-grounded multi-agent environment designed for training and evaluating medical diagnostic agents. Built on ClinPatient, a scalable dataset comprising 150k diagnostic cases derived from real-world electronic health records, ClinVerse supports coordinated interactions among six specialized clinical roles. Specifically, a doctor agent starts from an initial patient complaint, progressively gathers clinical evidence through patient interviews and examination requests, and ultimately produces a diagnosis. For each interaction trajectory, a rule-based scoring framework quantifies information acquisition, examination ordering, and diagnostic accuracy. These trajectory-level scores serve as reward signals for agent training while also enabling scalable evaluation. In experiments, we evaluate various general-purpose and medical-domain models and show that nine self-evolution methods across three categories consistently improve agents' diagnostic capabilities within ClinVerse. We further analyze the interplay among model capability, environment feedback, and self-evolution methods.

title: Multi-Agent Retrieval-Augmented Causality Assessment (MARCA) of Individual Case Safety Reports in Pharmacovigilance
summary:
Introduction: Increasing volumes of individual case safety reports (ICSRs) challenge expert-led causality assessment in pharmacovigilance. We developed MARCA (Multi-Agent Retrieval-Augmented Causality Assessment), a four-agent framework for Naranjo-based assessment, and evaluated agreement with human experts and exploratory differences between non-RAG and RAG-labelled scores.
  Methods: MARCA combined scientific literature retrieval, drug-label assessment, objective-evidence classification, and clinical causality reasoning using Gemini 2.5 Pro and DeepSeek-V3.2. Agent-generated rationales informed human-assisted scoring. A consensus expert reference standard covered 215 ICSRs and 1,562 drug-event combinations (DECs) from FAERS (Q1-Q2 2025). Agreement was measured using percentage agreement and Cohen's kappa.
  Results: Question-level agreement was 96.8% for Naranjo Q2 (kappa = 0.491; 95% CI 0.265-0.663), 85.4% for Q5 (kappa = 0.269; 95% CI 0.180-0.340), and 96.8% for Q10 (kappa = 0.922; 95% CI 0.885-0.951). Final causality classification agreement was 79.4% (95% CI 71.8-85.3; kappa = 0.587, 95% CI 0.450-0.690). In a retrospective subset of 60 DECs, agreement was higher for RAG-labelled than non-RAG scores for Q5 (83.3% vs 65.0%) and Q10 (100.0% vs 18.3%).
  Discussion: MARCA-assisted assessment showed substantial variation in agreement across Naranjo questions, with lower concordance for alternative causes. Retrospective RAG comparisons are exploratory and do not establish prospective effectiveness.

title: Distill, Debate, Discover: Grounding Multi-Agent Research Ideation in Graph-Distilled Insights
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support research idea generation and scientific discovery. Multi-agent debate offers a collaborative approach to this task by bringing together diverse perspectives to develop research ideas. However, a key challenge is how to equip agents with distinct and meaningful expertise to guide their contributions. Inspired by how researchers draw on accumulated research experience during collaboration, we introduce InsightAgents, a framework that constructs literature-grounded agent expertise by distilling insights from graphs of related papers. Guided by insights that trace evolving research approaches, reveal underlying assumptions, and identify unresolved challenges, within a line of research, agents jointly identify a research problem and propose, challenge, and refine potential approaches through debate to develop a research proposal. We evaluate InsightAgents against three research idea generation frameworks on 100 NLP research topics through pairwise comparisons by two LLM judges. In both online and offline knowledge settings, InsightAgents achieves the highest average score across the five evaluation dimensions under both judges.

title: Recursive Semantic Divergence for LLM Agent Consistency
comment: Accepted as a conference paper in NeurIPS 2026. Source code is publicly available in the repository in https://github.com/AgentConsistency/RSD-agent-consistency
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents with tool use exhibit inconsistent behavior across independent runs from identical states, calling different tools, producing contradictory outputs, or pursuing divergent strategies. This variability compounds over time and undermines deployment reliability. Existing evaluation metrics primarily measure task correctness via completion-based scores and do not capture consistency in agent behavior across executions. Separately, agent behavior is analyzed either at the token level using probability distributions or at the single-response level using semantic clustering, but neither captures how inconsistency propagates across future turns of a trajectory. We introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), an unsupervised trajectory-level consistency metric adapted from bisimulation metrics in reinforcement learning. RSD measures the expected cumulative semantic disagreement between two independent rollouts of the same agent from the same state, using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistency. It is defined recursively over future states and approximated by a neural network trained on independent rollouts. The learned metric estimates future divergence from the current state, providing a consistency score at each turn without requiring the full trajectory to complete. When used as a reward signal for fine-tuning, RSD reduces the variation in task progress from 132% to 91% on tau2-bench and from 90% to 44% on toolsandbox, while improving performance across benchmarks and model scales. Training with RSD as an additional reward signal matches supervised fine-tuning performance with substantially lower variance, without requiring ground-truth labels.

title: SLICE-Mem: Salience-Gated Lightweight Information Curation for Efficient LLM Agent Memory
summary: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to maintain personalized and temporally coherent interactions, but repeated LLM inference for memory admission, extraction, and organization introduces substantial cost and latency. We present SLICE-Mem, a lightweight memory framework that combines salience-guided admission and predicate-centered information extraction. A compact classifier identifies user turns worth retaining, and a semantic-dependency-based extractor converts admitted turns into concise memory entries. This online pipeline requires no generative LLM calls, while cross-entry reconciliation is deferred to an offline consolidation stage. We evaluate SLICE-Mem on the weekly subset of Memora and LongMemEval-S using 8B and 30B Qwen backbones for memory construction and consolidation on both benchmarks. Compared with the generative-memory baseline MemOS under the Qwen3-30B configuration, SLICE-Mem's online pipeline achieves 46.60 versus 46.68 FAMA (Forgetting-Aware Memory Accuracy) on Memora Weekly and 56.8% versus 59.3% accuracy on LongMemEval-S, while reducing total LLM token consumption by 92.4% and 99.5%, respectively. These results demonstrate that SLICE-Mem can preserve useful evidence for long-term memory with substantially less reliance on LLM-based memory construction.

title: Position, Role or Label? A Controlled Study of Instruction Conflicts in LLM Agents
comment: 55 pages, 8 figures, 24 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/anishh15/WhoWins (pip install whowins). Website: https://anishh15.github.io/WhoWins/
summary: LLM agents take instructions from the operator, repository configuration, user, tool results and saved memory, which often conflict. Instruction-hierarchy benchmarks ask whether the higher-ranked source wins, but a source sets position, role and label at once. First, we build WhoWins, 1,080 code-scored scenarios in five task types, each with up to five mutually exclusive instructions, and seven controlled experiments that vary only how instructions are delivered. Second, we study 14 open-weight models (0.6B to 122B, thinking off and on) over 1,887,356 scored replies, checking main findings on held-out scenarios. Inside one message the first of two conflicting lines wins 72.42 to 94.66%, and across messages it keeps 22.95 to 62.65%. A policy sent first in the system (or developer) message loses most conflicts with later lines in every Qwen model but wins most on gpt-oss when it acts. In tool and file-write tasks it wins less often than the same text sent first as a labelled user message, in every model-mode. Third, we test whether pairs forecast larger conflicts; forecasts improve in every model-mode once they know where the task line is. Finally, by our keyword patterns at most 2.92% of decided pair replies flag or hedge a conflict.

title: FlexA-Mem: Budget-Adaptive Agentic Memory for LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents work in scenarios with very different memory needs. A question about past conversations needs the exact facts it names, while a multi-step task needs a trace of the steps already taken together with details that the next step cannot name. Existing memories are each designed and tested for one kind of scenario. Retrieval memories such as A-Mem miss steps that the current query does not express, summaries drop exact strings, and pairing the two fixes the split of the budget in advance. We propose FlexA-Mem, a general memory that writes each unit of history once into an immutable store and renders a fresh memory for every call. The rendered memory is a compact timeline of records plus detail that a fixed rule fits into the remaining room without an LLM call. The detail is either relevant units as raw text or excerpts or the verbatim pieces that best match the query. With one store, FlexA-Mem serves both kinds of scenario. On AppWorld challenge tasks at 4k, it outperforms the second-best method by 11.5%, and on 147 unused tasks with predictions fixed in advance it outperforms A-Mem with a summary by 12.2%. On LongMemEval and LoCoMo, it matches a dedicated keyword retriever that writes no memory, while memories built on text written by an LLM fall far behind at tight budgets. Ablations show that the timeline carries AppWorld completion, whereas recovery mainly saves steps there and decides accuracy on exact facts. Code is available at https://github.com/WujiangXu/Flex-Amem

title: Trajectory2Gym: Decision-Grounded Compositional Interaction Synthesis for Tool-Use Agents
summary: Successful tool-use trajectories are not necessarily useful supervision. Even successful interactions may underrepresent multi-step dependencies or contain actions that are unjustified by the information visible to the agent at decision time. We identify two coupled requirements for effective trajectory supervision: compositional coverage, so that important observation-action dependencies are represented, and decision grounding, so that each supervised action is supported by the learner-visible interaction history. We introduce Trajectory2Gym, which constructs executable interactions around under-supported compositional structures and derives supervision only from grounded decisions in their realized executions. Structural-support selection allocates the resulting experience, while parent-normalized supervised fine-tuning preserves the semantic interaction as the unit of training weight. This reframes trajectory generation as the deliberate construction of learnable interaction experience, rather than the collection of successful trajectories. Across five Qwen3 scales, Trajectory2Gym improves Tau1, Tau2, and BFCL at every tested scale, increasing the equal-weight three-benchmark mean by 16.9-29.8 percentage points. The gains are strongest in stateful and multi-turn interaction, where later decisions depend on earlier observations and feedback. Our results suggest that scaling tool-use agents depends not only on collecting more successful trajectories, but on constructing interactions whose dependencies are represented and whose decisions are learnable from the agent's visible history.

title: Memory Tax: Dissecting the Net Value of Agent Memory
summary: Memory is increasingly used in long-horizon agents, yet the net value of building memory over direct retrieval from raw history remains largely unclear. Through a large-scale evaluation across multiple benchmarks and model backbones, we find many dedicated memory systems underperform naive RAG in many cases, indicating a negative net value. Taking RAG as a reference, we dissect the net value of memory into the gains and losses over direct retrieval, termed memory benefit and memory tax. These gains and losses arise because memory process changes how the raw information is organized and accessed. We view such changes as the double-edged deviations from the raw history. They are originally designed and introduced to benefit the task, for example by reorganizing facts or distilling preferences, but some may also remove or obscure evidence, giving rise to memory tax. Since memory benefit reflects the expected gains of its design, we then focus more on the overlooked memory tax, study how it arises from the system and evaluation side, and generalize the concept to more application scenarios of memory. We hope the notion of memory tax can provide a new lens and shift more attention from standalone performance to the net value of memory, informing more reliable memory designs and evaluations. We will open-source the code and results to the community. Project Page: https://hexuan21.github.io/MemoryTax/

title: Identically Trained Language Models Break on Different Jailbreaks
summary: Jailbreak benchmarks test one checkpoint and treat which jailbreaks break it as a property of its pretraining data and safety training. We ask whether another pretraining run of the same data, given the same safety training, would break on the same jailbreaks. For each of 25 pretraining data recipes, we take 1B base models from 3 pretraining seeds and give each the same safety post-training with 2 post-training seeds, for 150 models in all. We then collect 20 responses from every model to a shared set of jailbreak prompts and correlate the per-prompt non-refusal rates between every pair of models. On average, two post-trained copies of the same pretraining run have per-prompt non-refusal rates that correlate at 0.984. A different pretraining seed lowers the correlation to 0.811, and a different data recipe lowers it only slightly further, to 0.779. These results indicate that which jailbreaks break a checkpoint depends much more on its pretraining run than on its data, a pattern that holds in all 25 data recipes and at 150M and 300M parameters. In practice, the best of 91 attack templates found on one checkpoint stays the best after a new pretraining seed in only 27% of model pairs, against 67% after a new post-training seed. Each pretraining run also leaves a fingerprint: across 3,211 prompts, a model's per-prompt non-refusal rates identify its pretraining run among all 75 runs every time, and a random subset of 50 prompts still does so 98% of the time.

title: $Δτ$-Bench: Pushing Agents Toward a Moving Capability
summary: In this paper, we introduce $Δτ$-Bench, an executable agent benchmark that models the structural evolution of large tool ecosystems. In $Δτ$-Bench, independently evolving services continually reshape how tasks can be accomplished: familiar tools may disappear or be replaced, while more efficient alternatives emerge amid overlapping functionality and noisy documentation. Against this moving capability frontier, we evaluate whether agents can proactively discover efficient tool-use paths and promptly revise their accumulated procedural knowledge, bringing together demands that existing benchmarks fail to examine. $Δτ$-Bench comprises 1,588 validated multi-turn tasks across 42 domains and six successive ecosystem states generated through capability-preserving transformations. Our evaluation shows that even the strongest evaluated model or harness achieves only 42.3% task success, while initial gains from existing skill-learning methods can not consistently translate into better adaptation as the ecosystem evolves. These findings motivate Steward, an ecosystem manager that jointly manages tools and procedural knowledge through incremental skill maintenance and dynamic provisioning during task execution. Experiments show that Steward sustains higher task success across ecosystem changes with lower skill-maintenance overhead, while improving both recovery from disrupted workflows and adoption of more efficient alternatives.

title: From Instructions to Exploits: Applying Program Analysis to Malicious Agent Skills Across Natural Language and Code
summary: LLM-powered agents increasingly rely on third-party skills that combine natural-language instructions with executable code, creating supply-chain risks that may span both artifacts. Existing skill scanners often rely on rule matching or direct LLM judgments and provide limited support for tracing such cross-domain behavior. We present the Supply-Chain Scanner for Agent Skills (SCS), a static analysis framework that unifies instructions and code for security analysis. SCS compiles natural-language instructions into a constrained Python-style intermediate representation using a limited set of security-oriented APIs. It then constructs program dependence graphs for instructions and bundled code and connects them into a cross-domain graph (xPDG). A Trust-Sensitivity-Capability (TSC) model propagates security properties over the graph to support structured, largely deterministic risk detection. On a manually verified benchmark of 117 malicious and 117 benign skills, SCS achieves the highest average accuracy (85.6%), recall (95.2%), and F1-score (86.9%) among evaluated methods across five LLMs, with 80.2% precision and average token consumption of 13.7 million. Its NL-to-IR compiler achieves 92.5%-94.5% step-level correctness on 400 human-annotated instruction steps. Finally, analyzing 66,157 real-world ClawHub skills yields 2,473 candidates, of which 627 are confirmed malicious through auxiliary dynamic validation and manual review.

title: SentryBench: A Cost-Sensitive Benchmark for Adversarial Robustness of Tool-Using LLM Agents in Public-Safety Deployments
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly wired to consequential tools that send public alerts, dispatch responders, and query citizen records, where one erroneous tool call carries real-world cost. Existing agent-safety benchmarks measure generic harm or prompt-injection success and implicitly treat refusing as the safe default. In public-safety deployments that assumption breaks: an agent too cautious to dispatch help fails as surely as one that triggers a false alert. We present SentryBench, which scores agents on a two-sided, cost-sensitive frontier jointly measuring attack success, over-refusal (missing a real emergency), and over-reaction (unwarranted action) under adversarial tool use, with scenarios grounded in real emergency-call transcripts, disaster messages, and real injection/jailbreak payloads. We formalize deployment harm as an asymmetric cost functional, prove naive caution is harm-dominated whenever it refuses more genuine emergencies than the attack harm it averts, and prove a targeted trust gate adds zero over-refusal on clean input. Across 840 scored episodes over three frontier models and three defenses, refuse-more caution drives over-refusal to 100 percent on two of three models for at most a 3.7-point change in attack success and yields the worst harm everywhere, whereas our trust-gating wrapper dominates the frontier (lowest harm on every model, over-refusal at or below baseline, higher containment). Provider content filters also silently perform part of the defending and must be reported separately.

title: The Target Agent Is Its Own Best Critic but a Poor Proposer: Self-Improved Red Teaming
summary: Automatic red teaming increasingly relies on large language models (LLMs) to iteratively diagnose failed attacks and propose improved adversarial prompts or injections. Although prior work strengthens this loop through prompt engineering and search-harness design, the mechanisms underlying its two core roles, criticism and attack proposal, has not been explored. To further investigate the core roles and therefore improve red teaming effectiveness, we disentangle two design choices: whether criticism is generated by the target session itself (self-criticism) or by a separately instantiated critic (external criticism), and whether that criticism is translated into the next attack by the target session (self-proposal) or by a separate attacker (external proposal). Through our analysis, we find that self-criticism is more effective because it is grounded in the target's live execution context, including observations, constraints, and available reasoning; removing reasoning reduces downstream attack success by 6%-17%. In contrast, self-proposal is substantially less effective because awareness of the adversarial objective induces explicit refusal and non-refusal sandbagging. These findings motivate a role-separated red-teaming approach: the target session diagnoses why an attack failed, while a separately instantiated attacker generates the next proposal. On DTAP-BENCH, spanning Telecom, Workflow, CRM, and Code domains, under both direct misuse and indirect threat models, as well as multiple agent frameworks, this configuration achieves 63.2% overall attack success rate (ASR), much higher than baselines. Our results show that effective automatic red teaming depends not only on model capability and search strategy, but also on how execution context and adversarial responsibility are distributed across model sessions.

title: Then there is prompt injection, a malicious email, ...: The Wild Wide West of OpenClaw Agentic System Security
summary: AI-powered personal assistant frameworks such as OpenClaw combine LLM reasoning, persistent memory, tool invocation, local execution, and web-based workflows. These capabilities enable useful automation, but they also create security risks when untrusted inputs, model reasoning, tools, memory, and deployment configuration interact without explicit trust boundaries. This paper presents an empirical study of reported security concerns in OpenClaw using two complementary data sources: Reddit discussions and security-tagged GitHub issues. We analyze more than 25K Reddit posts from 13 OpenClaw-related subreddits and identify 162 security-relevant posts with 1,787 associated comments. We further collect 358 security-tagged GitHub issues and retain 180 issues describing concrete security concerns. Using qualitative analysis and evidence-grounded CWE mapping, we identify 521 CWE instances across 59 distinct weakness types, concentrated in access-control failures, sensitive-data exposure, injection, and unsafe execution. We also extract 543 practitioner mitigation suggestions and consolidate them into seven recurring strategies. To complement the empirical analysis, we present an evidence-grounded illustrative reconstruction of a representative sensitive-data exposure pathway using dummy secret values. Our findings show that OpenClaw security issues are not isolated implementation bugs; they reflect recurring trust-boundary failures across the agent execution pipeline. We discuss how these weaknesses map to both traditional software-security categories and agent-specific failure mechanisms, and derive implications for safer agentic systems, including explicit trust boundaries, least-privilege tool access, execution containment, runtime oversight, and defense-in-depth deployment.

title: Scope-Gap Injection: Exploiting Evaluator Channel Blind Spots in the OpenClaw Agent Security Competition
summary: This paper introduces Scope-Gap Injection (SGI), an indirect prompt injection method for multi-stage LLM-agent safety pipelines. In the IJCAI 2026 OpenClaw Agent Security Attack Competition, each attack package is judged by a static skill scan (S1), an LLM-judge safety check over the task and skill definition (S2), and a live execution audit (S3). Our observations suggest a scope gap: S2 appears to inspect the task instruction and skill definition without inspecting attachment contents, while the agent reads attachments during S3. SGI keeps the visible task and skill benign, while target identifiers, bypass parameters, and authorization procedures are moved into an attachment written as a business worklist. The S2 judge therefore sees a harmless task, while the agent follows the hidden worklist and triggers the permission bypass. In OpenClaw, SGI bypassed all three stages for 5 of 19 targets. The highest-scoring single submission achieved $F = 0.385$. Across the submission campaign, attachment placement was associated with higher aggregate S2 acceptance than in-skill placement: 78% versus 23%. We close with defenses that align evaluator scope with the channels available to the agent.

title: Hidden Backdoor Attack on Deep Contrastive Clustering
summary: Deep contrastive clustering has become a representative paradigm for unsupervised image clustering, yet its security under training-time poisoning remains largely unexplored. This paper investigates a hidden backdoor threat against deep contrastive clustering and proposes HBDCC, a Hidden Backdoor attack for Deep Contrastive Clustering. Here, hidden does not indicate that the trigger is visually imperceptible, but rather that the malicious trigger-cluster association remains behaviorally dormant on clean inputs and is activated only when the trigger appears at inference time. HBDCC poisons only a small fraction of unlabeled training samples and exploits an inherent structural weakness of contrastive clustering: augmentation-persistent triggers can be repeatedly aligned across different views at the instance level and further reinforced by cluster-level consistency objectives. As a result, the poisoned model preserves normal clustering behavior on clean data, while producing severely distorted cluster assignments for triggered inputs. We provide a dual-level analysis of the backdoor implantation mechanism and evaluate HBDCC on ImageNet-10, ImageNet-Dogs, and STL-10 with representative contrastive clustering frameworks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HBDCC can substantially degrade triggered clustering performance in a dataset-dependent manner while maintaining sufficient clean-data utility to evade standard evaluation protocols. We further conduct comprehensive studies on poisoning ratio, attack scope, trigger type, trigger size, and a lightweight knowledge-distillation-based mitigation strategy.

title: Spoofing the Toolbox: Optimizing Tool Descriptions to Deceive LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are widely used in many applications and often rely on external tools. Tool information, such as function descriptions, helps agents determine which tools best suit a given context. However, attackers can manipulate this information to mislead LLM agents into using malicious tools. Prior attacks mainly rely on keyword-based techniques, which are easily detected, or rule-based methods, which have limited effectiveness. In this work, we introduce TSA, a stealthy tool-spoofing attack that crafts descriptions for malicious tools that are difficult to distinguish from those of existing benign tools. To achieve this, we propose an LLM-powered optimization method that iteratively refines malicious tool descriptions. Specifically, TSA begins with a variant of a benign tool description and updates it based on feedback from a surrogate LLM agent. The optimization method incorporates a feedback function and contrastive in-context learning to guide the search for descriptions that are both stealthy and effective. Experiments on both single- and multi-tool use benchmarks demonstrate that TSA achieves an attack success rate of up to 92.13\%, outperforming four state-of-the-art approaches while remaining highly stealthy. Our user study further shows that even human participants cannot distinguish descriptions generated by TSA from benign ones. Moreover, TSA remains effective against five tool-malware detectors.

title: Alignment of Autonomous Cyber Defense Agents via Adaptive Policy Shaping
comment: Accepted to the Conference on Applied Machine Learning in Information Security
summary: Cybersecurity operators increasingly encounter sophisticated and fast-paced attacks, making autonomous cyber defense (ACD) a critical approach for supporting timely and effective decision-making. Reinforcement learning (RL)-based ACD agents have the ability to autonomously observe network states and take actions to defend and recover system assets, making them well suited for ACD. However, these agents often face critical trade-offs, such as improving network security while inadvertently degrading service availability or violating other operational priorities such as confidentiality and integrity, raising the core challenge of aligning agent behavior with human-specified goals and intent. In this work, we study the problem of aligning RL-based ACD agents with human-specified operational objectives without requiring costly retraining. We formalize alignment for ACD as a policy shaping problem, where a pretrained RL decision-making policy can be adjusted at test time using predicted attributes over agent actions. We also propose an adaptive approach that dynamically controls the alignment--performance trade-off as operational priorities shift during an ongoing cyber attack. We evaluate our method in a simulated cyber defense environment, CybORG, analyzing performance across multiple alignment objectives using the Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA) information security triad. Our results show that adaptive test-time policy shaping can significantly improve alignment while preserving core cyber defense performance, offering a practical and scalable alternative to training-time alignment methods in RL. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ITM-Kitware/alignment-cage-challenge-2.

title: A Deterministic Security Runtime for LLM Agents on MPI and Batch-Scheduled HPC Systems: Consensus-Governed, Hardware-Rooted Supervision of Every Rank
summary: Large language model agents launch simulations on high-performance computing (HPC) systems, where one sbatch or mpirun can commit thousands of node-hours and a forged result can cost lives. Of 23 surveyed systems, none supervises the running job, and none holds when the control host is compromised. We fix both. Enclawed, our deterministic security runtime for AI agents, has until now served a single user; this work makes it a distributed runtime for parallel HPC and agent swarms. The Enclaweder, our hardware root of trust, keeps a compromised host from becoming a catastrophe. A launch gate decides every launch by policy alone, refusing what it cannot parse. Once the job runs, a swarm chain grants short leases against signed heartbeats and evicts on evidence, and a supervisor around every rank pauses it when its lease lapses and kills it on tampering. Each node signs with its Enclaweder's key, so the host can forge none of it. Enclawed needs no administrator privileges and plugs into existing clusters unchanged, over Secure Shell alone. Supervision leaves the compute loop of a 16-rank LAMMPS job unchanged, on graphics processors too, and adds about 3 s of start-up. Twelve live attacks on Enclaweder-keyed ranks, colluding coordinators included, ended fail-closed. Sixteen agents on a real model attempted 24 launches that planted instructions ordered; the gate denied all 24 and allowed all 108 legitimate ones. Enclawed's core and the HPC Agent Security Benchmark are open source.

title: Intent-Preserving Adversarial User Simulation for Multi-Turn Agent Evaluation
summary: Multi-turn agents are commonly evaluated with LLM-based simulated users, which can be overly cooperative and can therefore overestimate an agent's performance. We here introduce StressSim, an intent-preserving adversarial user simulator framework for stress-testing agents with challenging yet valid user interactions. StressSim optimises the simulator's high-level adversarial plan for each task instance. Candidate planner prompts are evolved with a genetic prompt-optimisation loop that uses rollout traces, granular task-completion signals, and validity feedback to favour conversations that reduce task success without changing the user's underlying goal. We evaluate the approach on the MultiWOZ dataset and the retail and airline domains from tau-bench with three target LLM agents, comparing against standard simulators and hand-designed non-collaborative user behaviours. We demonstrate the effectiveness of StressSim in exposing robustness gaps across frontier LLMs, with tau-bench pass^4 scores decreasing by up to 69% on gemini-3.8-flash and 62% on gpt-5.6-sol. StressSim maintains goal preservation performance (which decreases by at most 10%), using an optimisation budget of 20 rollouts per task. Sensitivity analysis suggests that increasing the budget further decreases task success. Overall our results demonstrate that StressSim exposes robustness gaps missed by standard and hand-designed user simulators while maintaining conversation realism. This is achieved through lightweight prompt optimisation alone, without model fine-tuning.

title: Belief-Conditioned Multi-Agent Actor Critic for Decentralized LLM Collaboration
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop PTA: From Pretrained Representations to Acting Agents. 18 pages, 3 figures
summary: Recent work has explored optimizing LLM collaboration through Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), but many approaches still rely on predefined workflows, limiting efficiency and scalability. Decentralized LLM collaboration is challenging because agents execute independently with limited communication, share a joint objective, and must infer useful information from communication traces. In this paper, we propose BCMAAC, a Belief-Conditioned Multi-Agent Actor-Critic method that maintains beliefs over contextual information and uses them to facilitate training. Experiments on Minecraft game-playing, web searching and tool-using tasks show that BCMAAC improves task performance and collaborative behavior compared to naive actor-critic baselines. The improvements are particularly pronounced in multi-turn tasks with richer contextual information, where belief modeling provides a clear advantage.

title: Lessons from Luck: Do LLM-Written Lessons Carry Chance into an Agent's Next Decision?
comment: 28 pages, 1 figure, 11 tables. A registered study: the protocol, code and stimuli were frozen, deposited (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23253562) and timestamped in a Bitcoin block before the confirmatory run. The locked run records are public (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23272809)
summary: Self-improving agents write lessons from the outcomes of their runs; when outcomes are noisy, a lesson can carry chance into later decisions. We measure one link of this chain in a registered study. In 256 synthetic worlds, each a recurring task with two interchangeable tools of recorded reliability, a scripted previous run used the more reliable tool (a good decision) or the less reliable one (a bad decision), with an assigned outcome: success or a transient failure. A model wrote a lesson from the run with ReasoningBank's memory-writing instruction; a fresh session of the same model, holding the authoritative log and the previous result, chose the next run's first tool with one memory item: that lesson, the lesson from the other outcome, an irrelevant item, or an unreasoned directive. The protocol was frozen, deposited and timestamped before any confirmatory call; 11 LLM endpoints gave 90,084 answers. After a chance failure of the better tool, the panel's lessons carried the chance (registered reading luck-carrying; interaction +0.112, 95% interval [+0.097, +0.126]): readers named the worse tool in 11.6% of next runs with the lesson written from that failure, against 0.4% with an irrelevant item and 0.4% with the lesson written from a success. The effect was +0.042 where the log stated that failures are independent and +0.181 where it did not (descriptive). After a lucky success of the worse tool, the interaction was bounded below 0.10 (+0.002), a bound, not evidence of no harm. In exploratory readings, 6 endpoints carried the chance (up to +0.352); 5 were bounded below 0.10. In secondary comparisons, a three-sentence decision-quality note in the writing instruction lowered the worse-tool rate after a chance failure to 7.5%, and one instruction for both outcomes with a no-change option to 3.1%; neither met the registered harm-reduction rule at every such endpoint.

title: Augmentation-Guided Adversarial Training via Local Stability-Based Sample Selection
summary: Adversarial training remains one of the most effective defenses against adversarial attacks, but its standard PGD-based training is computationally expensive because adversarial examples are generated for every training sample. Selective adversarial training reduces this cost by perturbing only a subset of samples. However, existing selective techniques typically rely on point-wise difficulty signals such as loss, entropy, margin, or gradients. We show that these point-wise criteria do not capture local instability in a sample's neighborhood. Motivated by this, we propose Augmentation-Guided Adversarial Training (AGAT), a selective adversarial training framework that uses augmentation-induced local variation to allocate samples with unstable neighborhoods for adversarial training. AGAT ranks samples using Augmentation-based Local Stability (ALS), a lightweight score that measures the normalized change in model logits between an input and its label-preserving augmented variant. Experiments across different architectures on MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet-200 demonstrate that AGAT achieves comparable or higher robust accuracy while applying adversarial supervision to only 20-30% of the training samples in each minibatch. AGAT also requires less training time than all other adversarial training baselines in the computational cost evaluation.

title: From Intelligence to Autonomy: Foundations and Construction of Autonomous Agents for Future Intelligent Systems
summary: Artificial intelligence is moving from one-off perception and generation tasks toward long-term planning, tool use, and interaction with real environments. Greater task competence, however, does not automatically yield autonomy: an external actor may still have to set goals, sustain operating conditions, detect failures, and approve updates. We define an autonomous agent as a system that, within explicit identity and authority boundaries, maintains both task goals and viability conditions, acts continuously using models of the world and itself, and adjusts its control mechanisms and long-term capabilities through feedback. We trace the conceptual path from homeostasis and feedback control to autopoiesis and biological autonomy. We then distinguish six lines of operationalization: computational autopoiesis, behavior-based robotics, agent formalization, adaptive software, embodied adaptation, and robotic self-modeling. On this basis, we propose a one-boundary, four-loop framework in which Operational, Viability, Reflexive, and Learning loops organize task execution, self-maintenance, metacontrol, and governed learning. Five paired simulation experiments test permission constraints, road-closure response, health maintenance, capability re-estimation, and cross-task learning. Their results provide preliminary evidence for the feasibility of these mechanisms, while broader environments and physical systems remain to be tested.

title: Collective Collaboration of Recursive Autonomous Agents
summary: Smart factories must translate order-level objectives into production tasks at multiple scales and combine the capabilities of individual units into an overall delivery capability. To address repeated adaptation of organizational mechanisms across equipment, workshops, and factories, as well as coordination across levels under changing production conditions, this paper develops a framework for the collective collaboration of recursive autonomous agents (RAAs). A common task and capability interface supports the recursive decomposition of production objectives from the top down and the aggregation of conditional capabilities through peer collaboration from the bottom up. Composite units can therefore participate in higher-level organizations as agents of the same kind. We formulate organizational models for leaf and composite units, specify interface closure under composition and conditions for finite task expansion, and develop operational mechanisms linking task decomposition, resource commitments, result aggregation, and coordination within the scope affected by change. A production network integrating machining, inspection, and logistics across multiple workshops illustrates how a common organizational kernel is instantiated at the equipment-service, workshop, and factory scales. The framework connects recursive organization with explicit task responsibilities, capability conditions, and execution interfaces for manufacturing systems.

title: Continual Learning Exam: Benchmarking Long-Horizon RSI and Experiential Learning in LLM Agents
summary: Continual learning is the ability of LLM agents to improve over time by acquiring, refining, and applying knowledge from experience while retaining useful prior knowledge. It is essential for agents learning over long time horizons, yet current evaluations largely assess individual task performance rather than improvement through accumulated experience. We introduce Continual Learning Exam (CLE), a large-scale benchmark developed by 50+ domain experts to measure experience-driven improvement in realistic professional workflows. CLE comprises 120 human-authored tasks, each organised as a five-level ladder, yielding 600 levels spanning 89 professional roles across 12 occupational domains. Agents must pass each level to unlock the next, with later levels building on experience accumulated during earlier assignments. An evaluation agent assesses each submission against human-authored rubrics. We compare a single-submission setting with one that provides diagnostic feedback after failure and allows one revision. Across 17 harness-model configurations using frontier LLMs, feedback and revision yield a median completion gain of 5.3 percentage points. Yet the best-performing system clears only 47.7% of levels and completes all five levels in just 23.3% of tasks, highlighting the difficulty of sustained learning from experience for existing frontier LLMs. As such, the dataset can also be used to post-train LLMs to strengthen their continual learning capabilities.

title: Holding a Steady Course: Knowledge Evolution from Expertise and Lessons for Continual Agent Learning
summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly deployed across sequences of related tasks, yet they often fail to retain and improve their knowledge over time. Existing approaches convert interaction trajectories into memories or reusable skills, but experience is not automatically reliable knowledge. Automatically collected skills and memories can propagate errors, mislead, and corrupt useful knowledge. To address this gap, we introduce Knowledge Evolution from Expertise and Lessons (KEEL), an agent-agnostic framework that uses verifier evidence to transform successful behavior into reusable skills and failures into corrective lessons. As new evidence accumulates, individual skill claims can be supported, contradicted, replaced, or retired. On SkillFlow benchmark, KEEL improves task success by 4.2 to 21.7 percentage points over the no-knowledge baseline, compared with gains of 2.4 to 9.6 points from SkillFlow's default method. Ablations show that skills and lessons are complementary. These results show that reliable continual agent learning depends not simply on accumulating experience, but on continually validating and evolving the knowledge derived from it. Our code is available at: https://github.com/microsoft/KEEL-TTCL26.

title: Self-Evolution Reasoner: Continuous Optimization via Policy-Intrinsic Exploration and Exploitation
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) enables large language models (LLMs) to continuously self-improve their reasoning capabilities. Compared to RLVR's scalar rewards, recent self-supervised on-policy distillation methods leverage denser supervision signals. However, both paradigms suffer from exploration bottlenecks, struggling to escape local optima when the policy fails to sample valid solutions. Relying on external demonstrations can bypass this issue; however, the off-policy nature hinders genuine self-improvement and the mismatched-distribution reasoning can not be fully exploited. In this work, we propose Self-Evolution Policy Optimization (SEPO), a framework that drives continuous reasoning capability evolution via guided exploration and in-distribution exploitation. Specifically, SEPO utilizes labels to elicit correct reasoning from the policy, unlocking the exploration potential. By treating current policy conditioned on this in-distribution reasoning as a self-teacher, SEPO distills the newly discovered solution back into the policy. Through this iterative cycle of policy-intrinsic exploration and exploitation, SEPO achieves robust and continuous capability evolution. Across scientific, tool-use, and complex logical reasoning domains, SEPO consistently achieves the best performance under identical training time or steps, demonstrating superior efficiency and convergence ceilings. Notably, SEPO maintains stable improvements even in scenarios where baselines severely underperform or fail entirely, such as on complex tasks or with small-scale models. Our code is available at https://github.com/Eric8932/SEPO.

title: DoubleFree:Exploiting Exploration History for Rollout-Free Multi-Task LLMs Training
summary: Multi-task post-training can develop domain specialists through independent reinforcement learning (RL) and consolidate their capabilities through multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). However, standard MOPD generates on-policy student responses and keeps multiple teachers online throughout consolidation, introducing substantial system costs. We view this pipeline as domain-wise exploration followed by cross-domain exploitation. Domain RL produces not only the final specialists, but also the trajectories collected throughout their training. Existing methods primarily use the former while leaving the latter underutilized. We introduce DoubleFree, which reuses these historical trajectories for rollout-free consolidation and precomputes teacher supervision for online-teacher-free student training. To understand why this works, we analyze when updates from historical trajectories can approximate on-policy distillation updates and how combining trajectories across exploration stages can better support an evolving student. DoubleFree requires only minimal changes to existing post-training frameworks. Across math, code, and instruction following on Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and SmolLM3-3B, DoubleFree achieves $2.99$-$5.75\times$ consolidation speedups and reduces GPU-hours by $80.9$-$90.1\%$, while maintaining comparable multi-domain performance.
